The black cherry tree (Prunus serotina) is also known as the rum cherry because Appalachian pioneers used the fruit to flavor rum and brandy, creating a drink called cherry bounce.

"Black cherry is a leading cause of livestock illness, and grazing animals' access to it should be limited.

Uses
Known as capolcuahuitl in Nahuatl (the source of the capuli epithet), it was an important food in pre-Columbian Mexico. Native Americans ate the berries.[13]

The wood of Prunus serotina is also used as a spice in foods, as it imparts a unique flavor.

Prunus serotina timber is valuable; perhaps the premier cabinetry timber of the U.S., traded as "cherry". High quality cherry timber is known for its strong orange hues and high price. Low-quality wood, as well as the sap wood, can be more tan. Its density when dried is around 580 kg/m3 (36 lb/cu ft)."

Uses
Known as capolcuahuitl in Nahuatl (the source of the capuli epithet), it was an important food in pre-Columbian Mexico. Native Americans ate the berries.[13]

The wood of Prunus serotina is also used as a spice in foods, as it imparts a unique flavor.

Prunus serotina timber is valuable; perhaps the premier cabinetry timber of the U.S., traded as "cherry". High quality cherry timber is known for its strong orange hues and high price. Black Cherry is a medium sized deciduous tree, growing to 50-80 feet. The leaves are 2 to 5 inches long and shaped as an elongated oval. They are glossy and bright green, turning yellow in the fall. The flowers are small, white, and five petaled, giving rise to small reddish-black drupes. Depending on the region, they can flower from March to July, earlier in the spring in the south and later in the spring and summer in the north. Young trees have smooth, birch-like bark which becomes broken and dark gray to black with maturity. They range throughout the eastern half of the United States. It is a pioneer species and can be found growing in old fields and other places where sunlight is readily available. White-tailed deer eat the leaves.

description: Abundance: common

This is a black cherry tree (Prunus Serotina) which is a very common tree in western PA. You can tell this by its alternating, oval, serrated, and pointed end leaf shape. The leaves are about 3-5 inches long. Another give away is it’s rough bark. This picture was taken on a very sunny and 75 degree day last week. Along with this tree, I also saw a pin oak (quercus palustris) and a Norway maple (Acer platanoides). I am unsure of the relationships that these species have but I know that It is not uncommon to see these three species together in this part of the country.

I saw this Black Cherry tree (Prunus serotina) alongside a sidewalk on campus next to a shaded wooded area, you can tell it is a Black Cherry based on its oval like leaves that come to a point with serrated margins and the orange hairs on the base of the leaves, along with its rough “crispy” bark. The weather that day was 72° F, the high was 73°F and the low was 61°F. There was a light drizzle at the time with 69% humidity and sse 6 mph winds. Other species seen nearby were the Tree of Heaven (Ailanthus altissima) and Tulip Tree (Liriodendron tulipifera).

description:
With Valeri Ponzo; Day 1 of our 3-day Thanksgiving holiday trip to the eastern Panhandle.

Our itinerary for Day 1 was:

0832-0948 EST: Forest Capital Museum State Park (Taylor County) -- our 71st state park birded together.

1041-1332 CST: Three Rivers State Park (Jackson County) -- our 72nd state park birded together.

1417-1710 CST: Chipola River Water Management Area (Calhoun County)

We spent the night at the Palmer Motel in Miday (only $44 with a $30 discount from booking.com!).

The weather at this site was cloudy and 65 degrees with a light breeze. We left at 0948.

We barely saw the sun on any of the three days; most photographs were taken under gloomy skies, which meant that I often had to boost the light saturation to get a usable image, even if the inage ended up looking washed-out.

description: This little 2 foot tall cherry seedling is volunteering in a patch of *Amsonia* in a flowerbed, I'm sure planted by birds. Offhand, I don't know of any mature ones on my property, but the seedlings pop up frequently. Even though this plant is small, it still has several traits that help with family and genus identification. Woody growth, alternate leaves, stipules (paired flaps of tissue at the leaf bases), and serrated leaf margins are all traits typical of the rose family, to which cherries belong. Glands on the petioles of the leaves (those little lumps along the leaf stalks) probably secrete sugar water when the leaves are young to help encourage ants to guard the new growth. These aren't found in similar-looking relatives like apples, pears, and carbapples. These glands are a sign you have the genus *Prunus* (cherries, nectarines, peaches, apricots). Wild black cherry is our most common *Prunus* in local woods. Usually, the undersides of the leaves have about 1/2" of rusty hairs along the midvein, which is a useful ID trait, but it varies, and this plant doesn't have any.

description:
This is a black cherry tree or prunus serotina. This tree was still fairly young reaching a height of around 6ft with a very thin trunk. The bark was shiny and fissured, while the leaves are described as: bright green, alternate, simple, with finely toothed edges. Typically, this tree has fruit that are berry-like, but I didn't see any.

The weather when finding this tree was 69F with a high of 79F and a low of 59F. It was mostly cloudy with the wind being 6 mph and the humidity being 67%.

An interesting specie interaction that I noticed, but didn't get a picture of, is the black cherry fungus (black knot) or apiosporina morbosa. It's a common fungal disease seen on prunus trees, but it was especially interesting that it was on a tree as young as the one I found. Found on branches and sometimes trunks, it looks like a black bumpy growth that can encase what it grows on. The symptoms of when a tree is really suffering range from leaves starting to brown to it infecting the inside of the tree causing it to rot.

description:
Prunus serotina (Black Cherry)

Found at 12:08pm on 06OCT2023

Weather: Partly Cloudy, 67F, High 70F, Low 54F, .8" of rain in the last 24hrs, Wind 7mph NE

Other Species in the area: Acer nigrum (Black Maple), Malus domestica (Apple), Parthenocissus quinquefolia (Virginia Creeper), Rubus occidentalis (Black Raspberry), Rosa multiflora (Multiflora Rose)

The fruit of this Prunus serotina or Black Cherry is a dead giveaway as to what species this tree is. While beyond ripe and hard to capture with a camera, the small black cherries hang among the branches. The simple, alternate, finely serrated leaves provide more evidence that this is indeed a Black Cherry. If that's not enough, a closer look at the leaning trunk that doesn't appear to taper (another characteristic of Black Cherries) will show that it has round scales of bark that help to differentiate it from other types of cherry trees.

This tree in particular sits comfortably at the edge of a mowed yard and uses its tendency to lean to reach out from underneath other trees toward the sunlight. The long hanging branch of this tree is a favorite of the local bird population (Turdus migratorius/American Robin, Cyanocitta cristata/Blue Jay, and Zenaida macroura/Mourning Dove) for perching.

Some understory species such as Parthenocissus quinquefolia (Virginia Creeper), Rubus occidentalis (Black Raspberry), and Rosa multiflora (Multiflora Rose) enjoy ample space beneath this leaning tree.

Prunus serotina, commonly called black cherry, wild black cherry, rum cherry, or mountain black cherry, is a deciduous tree or shrub of the genus Prunus. Despite being called black cherry, it is not very closely related to the commonly cultivated cherries such as sweet cherry (P. avium), sour cherry (P. cerasus) and Japanese flowering cherries (P. serrulata, P. speciosa, P. sargentii, P. incisa, etc.) which belong to Prunus subg. Cerasus. Instead, P. serotina belongs to Prunus... (Source: Wikipedia, Prunus_serotina, CC BY-SA 3.0) 

"Dark Side of a Black Cherry" 
https://www.treehugger.com/identify-black-cherry-1341850 
"The leaves, twigs, bark and seeds of black cherry produce a chemical called cyanogenic glycoside. Hydrogen cyanide is released when the living parts of plant material are chewed and eaten and are toxic to both human and animal. It has a very repulsive taste and that taste is one of the identifying factors of the tree.
"Most poisoning comes from livestock eating wilted leaves, which contain more of the toxin than fresh leaves but with a diminishing of the bad taste. Interestingly enough, white-tailed deer browse seedlings and saplings without harm.
"The inner bark has highly concentrated forms of the chemical but was actually used ethnobotanically..."

description:
A solo visit to check on the Sparkleberry bushes. They're just starting to bloom, so the next 1-3 weeks should be great for hairstreaks. There were lots of lupines, pawpaws, and especially Lyreleaf Sages blooming. Butterflies were scarce but I photographed four species of moths. Variable Dancers were common; I quit photographing them after the 4th one encountered. I walked the usual trails in clockwise order, since I wanted to visit the main Sparkleberry patch first. I used my camera to take macro photographs, and after about 15 minutes of last using it, I realized that my phone was not in my pocket. I remembered where I last used it and back-tracked my path right to the phone.

Surprisingly, there were few vehicles in the parking lot at my arrival, and no mother truckers on the mound. (Did somebody from FWC or SWFWMD finally tell the mother truckers that a state preserve is not appropriate for them to run their r/c vehicles over the area?). Several people were crossing Aripeka Road to go swimming in the pond to the south. 

The weather at my arrival was sunny and 79 degrees ("feels like" 82) -- both temperatures seemed low -- with a light breeze. The weather when I left was one degree warmer, which again seemed too low. I left at 1717 after exactly 3 hours and headed home.
